title: Auto-rollback on SLO breach — PRD notes (working doc)
content:
Context / why this doc exists
- This is the messy PRD scratchpad before we freeze a Confluence PRD.
- Purpose: capture open questions, customer anecdotes, defaults, UX expectations, and the tradeoffs we need to align on.
- In-scope: auto-rollback on latency + error-rate SLO breach for model/version rollouts.
- Out-of-scope: automatic roll-forward; LLM output-quality regressions (separate quality gates).

Primary user problem (plain language)
- “We shipped a new model version to 5–20% traffic, it got worse, but we didn’t notice fast enough or couldn’t revert quickly/confidently.”
- Operators want a safety net that is predictable and auditable.
- Need to avoid rollback flapping, and avoid mass rollbacks during correlated incidents.

Who is asking for it (customer voice)
1) Enterprise reliability owner (SUP-18421 + HubSpot 49201)
- Incident: latency spike during a model rollout (Dedicated + strict SLOs). They had to page multiple teams, revert manually, and do a retro.
- Quote from notes (paraphrased): “We don’t want humans in the critical path for obvious regressions. Rollback should be policy-driven and logged.”
- Key asks:
  - per-region thresholds (they see EU-west behaving differently)
  - audit trail exported to SIEM (who/what rolled back, and why)
  - explicit controls to pause auto-rollback during known incidents

2) Dedicated prospect (HubSpot 49244 + Fireflies ff-90113)
- Theme: change-management + predictability.
- They want canary to feel “safe” and want proof we won’t thrash traffic splits.
- Key asks:
  - cooldowns + minimum traffic requirements
  - “worse than baseline” logic (don’t rollback if baseline also degraded)
  - strong “why” explanation in UI (verdict + metrics snapshot)

3) False positive complaint (SUP-18457)
- Customer reported unexpected rollback; suspected monitor staleness + low traffic. They perceived it as “random.”
- Takeaway: we must treat monitor quality as a first-class input and have an ‘unknown’/‘insufficient data’ verdict.

High-level product decision: what are we promising?
- Automatic rollback is not “perfect autopilot.” It is a guardrail with explicit guardrails.
- We should be explicit in UI/copy:
  - requires enough traffic + stable monitors
  - may not trigger if data is missing or ambiguous
  - never triggers infinite loops (cooldown and rate limits)

Success metrics (rough, not final)
- Reduce time-to-revert (TTR) for bad rollouts:
  - Target: rollback initiated within 3–5 minutes of clear breach on canary traffic (for high-volume routes).
- Reduce customer-impact minutes during rollout incidents (proxy = duration of elevated latency/error while canary is live).
- Reduce oncall manual actions for common regressions.
- Guardrail metric: false positive rollback rate (need a definition): e.g., rollbacks later marked as “not needed” / “monitor issue” / “correlated incident” by oncall.

Definitions / terms (so we stop talking past each other)
- “Rollout”: a change in model version for a route (or route+customer tier+region), typically via canary or A/B split.
- “Stable version”: last known-good model version pinned for that route.
- “Verdict”: controller’s current evaluation state for candidate (healthy/unhealthy/unknown) + reason.
- “Unknown”: we cannot evaluate due to missing/stale monitors or insufficient traffic.
- “Baseline”: stable version metrics (same route/tier/region) during the evaluation window.

What triggers rollback? (candidate policy knobs)
We likely need these knobs, but we should decide what is configurable vs fixed.

Proposed core policy fields (configurable)
- metrics: latency and error-rate (two independent signals, either can trigger)
- threshold style: fixed threshold vs burn-rate
  - TBD which ships first; see tradeoffs section.
- evaluation window(s): short window + confirm window (e.g., 2m + 5m) or a single window with “N of M datapoints”
- minimum traffic: minimum requests in window (or minimum RPS) before we trust the signal
- warm-up delay: ignore first X minutes after rollout starts (avoid cold cache, model load, batcher stabilization)
- cooldown: after rollback, do not attempt to rollback again for Y minutes (avoid flapping)
- “must be worse than baseline”: only rollback if candidate is worse than stable by a delta or ratio
- fail behavior when monitoring is down/stale: fail-open vs fail-closed (more below)

Proposed defaults (first pass; needs SRE review)
NOTE: These are “safe-ish” defaults for typical hosted routes; Dedicated may want tighter.

Latency rollback defaults
- metric: p95 end-to-end latency (or p95 model latency?) — open question below.
- threshold: p95 > 1.25x SLO target for window (or > absolute ms)
- window: 5 minutes evaluation
- datapoint requirement: 3 consecutive evaluation intervals (1m granularity) or “breach for 3 of last 5 minutes”
- minimum traffic: 300 requests per 5 minutes (or 1 RPS sustained) — need to sanity check across long-tail routes
- warm-up delay: 7 minutes after first traffic to candidate
- must-be-worse-than-baseline: candidate p95 is > baseline p95 by >= 20% AND baseline itself is within its own SLO (to avoid global incidents triggering rollback)
- cooldown after rollback: 30 minutes

Error rollback defaults
- metric: 5xx rate (and possibly 429?) — open question.
- threshold: 5xx > 1% (Hosted) / 0.5% (Dedicated) for 5 minutes (placeholder)
- minimum traffic: 500 requests in window (to avoid one-off spikes)
- warm-up delay: 5 minutes (maybe shorter than latency?)
- must-be-worse-than-baseline: yes (candidate error > baseline error + 0.3% absolute)
- cooldown: 30 minutes

Rate limits / blast radius (guardrails)
- Global guardrail: do not execute more than N auto-rollbacks per region per 10 minutes (protect against correlated incident or monitor bug).
- Per-tenant guardrail: max 1 rollback per tenant per route per cooldown.
- “Stop the bleeding” vs “don’t mass-flip”: we probably need both.

Open questions (PRD blockers)
1) Which latency metric is authoritative for rollback?
- Options:
  - end-to-end request latency (what customer sees)
  - model execution latency (runtime only)
  - “time-to-first-token” (TTFT) for streaming routes
- My current leaning: end-to-end p95 for rollback decisions, but we need a debugging breakdown in the UI.
- Concern: end-to-end includes upstream network issues; this increases correlated-incident rollbacks.
- Mitigation: baseline comparison + correlated incident detection? (but we said no new monitoring system)

2) Which error signals count?
- 5xx only? include 429 (rate limiting) / 408 timeouts?
- Dedicated customers consider timeouts as “errors.”
- Risk: 429 triggers rollback during capacity incidents; but rollback won’t fix that.

3) What is the unit of policy attachment?
- Per route? per route+model? per route+customer tier? per region?
- We keep hearing “per-region thresholds” (SUP-18490).
- Practical: start with route + candidate model + region + tier (and allow wildcards in policy schema).

4) “Fail-open vs fail-closed” when monitoring is unavailable
- Fail-open: do not rollback if we can’t evaluate (reduces false positives), but can increase time with bad candidate if monitors are broken.
- Fail-closed: rollback when monitors are missing/stale (conservative), but can cause mass rollbacks from monitoring outage.
- Current direction from architecture thread: default fail-open + surface ‘unknown’ verdict + alert on monitor fetch failure.
- We might allow per-tenant override for regulated Dedicated?

5) How do we avoid flapping without making rollback too slow?
- Warm-up + minimum traffic + cooldown is the basic package.
- Additional idea: require “confirmed breach” (short window) then “sustained breach” (longer window) before rollback.

6) Baseline comparison semantics
- “must be worse than baseline” is popular but tricky.
- Do we require baseline to be “healthy” (within SLO) or just compare candidate vs baseline regardless?
  - If baseline is unhealthy, rolling back doesn’t help.
- Proposed: baseline must be within SLO OR candidate must be worse than baseline by a large margin (escape hatch).

7) Multi-signal behavior
- If latency breaches but errors are fine, do we rollback? yes.
- If latency OK but errors breach, yes.
- Do we combine with weights or just OR? Probably OR for v1.

8) How does this interact with manual overrides in Console?
- Need:
  - pause auto-rollback for this rollout (temporary)
  - acknowledge a rollback event (to stop paging?)
  - force rollback now (manual)
  - lock traffic split (prevent automation from changing it)
- Need to define who can do what (RBAC), especially for enterprise.

9) What do we show in Console so this doesn’t feel like a black box?
- Must show:
  - current policy (resolved policy after wildcards)
  - current verdict (healthy/unhealthy/unknown)
  - last evaluation timestamps and inputs (window, traffic, monitor freshness)
  - “reason” text including breached metric + threshold + baseline value
  - rollback history timeline: what happened + links
- Nice-to-have:
  - evaluation trace / debug view (“why didn’t it rollback?”)

10) Monitor identity contract / labeling gaps
- We have an internal dependency: missing metric labels in some services (INT-3310).
- If labels are inconsistent, controller can’t find the right monitor and verdict becomes unknown.
- We need a migration plan and a UI indicator when monitor identity is not satisfied.

Tradeoffs to settle (needs Marissa + SRE alignment)
A) Burn-rate vs fixed thresholds
- Burn-rate pros:
  - conceptually aligns with error budgets and is standard SRE approach
  - can be more robust across services with different baselines
- Burn-rate cons:
  - harder to explain to customers/operators
  - requires accurate SLO objective definitions and good windowing
- Fixed threshold pros:
  - easy to explain (“p95 > 900ms for 5m”)
  - straightforward config
- Fixed threshold cons:
  - can be brittle across tiers and evolving SLO targets

Current proposal:
- v1 ship fixed thresholds + baseline comparison + cooldown.
- Keep door open for burn-rate in follow-up (ENG-2314).

B) Default behavior for low-volume routes
- If minimum traffic not met: do NOT rollback (unknown verdict). However, this means some long-tail regressions won’t trigger.
- Alternative: allow “minimum RPS” to be very low, but higher false positives.
- We should message clearly: auto-rollback is optimized for routes with sufficient traffic.

C) Auto-rollback scope during correlated incidents
- Without a global incident signal, we must rely on baseline comparison + rate limiting.
- Rate limiting is essential (per region + global), otherwise one network event flips a bunch of rollouts.

D) Dedicated vs Hosted defaults
- Dedicated wants:
  - tighter SLOs, per-region thresholds
  - more aggressive rollback
  - sometimes fail-closed (!) but risky
- Hosted wants:
  - avoid false positives + avoid noisy rollbacks affecting many tenants
- Likely solution: tier-specific default policies + per-tenant overrides.

UX notes / copy ideas (from product Slack thread)
- “Verdict” terminology: might be too SRE-y, but it’s concise.
  - Alternatives: “Health check result” / “Auto-rollback status”
- Keep the main UI simple:
  - Status: Healthy / At risk / Rolling back / Rolled back / Unknown
  - One-line reason: “Latency p95 breached: 980ms > 800ms (5m window). Baseline 620ms.”
  - Button: “Pause auto-rollback” and “View details”
- Details drawer should show:
  - chart snippets (latency + error), baseline overlay
  - evaluation settings + resolved monitor identity
  - last 10 evaluation cycles with input values (helps SRE debug)

Notification expectations (from SRE)
- Slack notification should include:
  - route, model version, region/tier, prior stable version
  - reason + metric snapshot
  - link to rollout page + runbook + dashboard
- Paging policy:
  - do we page on every auto-rollback? Probably not.
  - maybe page only if rollback fails, or if repeated rollbacks occur (indicates systemic issue).
  - otherwise create ticket / Slack-only.

Audit / compliance notes (Naomi + Marcus inputs)
- Every automated rollback must be attributable to:
  - policy ID/version
  - monitor identity used
  - evaluation window + metric values
  - actor = “rollout-controller” (service principal) + correlation ID
- Also need audit events for:
  - policy changes
  - manual override/pause/ack
  - rollback executor action (traffic split revert) including before/after.

Edge cases list (please add)
- Monitor stale/unavailable -> verdict unknown; ensure we don’t rollback just because of this.
- Monitor points delayed (telemetry lag) -> could trigger late rollback after issue resolved.
- Baseline also degrades -> do not rollback (unless candidate is significantly worse).
- Canary has tiny traffic -> no rollback, but UI should say “insufficient data.”
- Rollback fails (routing service error) -> escalate; retry with idempotency key.
- Multiple concurrent rollouts on same route (should we disallow? how to evaluate?)
- A/B experiments: if multiple variants, what is “stable”?

Proposed rollout plan (draft)
- Phase 0: internal canaries only, feature-flagged.
- Phase 1: opt-in for low-risk hosted tenants + a couple Dedicated design partners.
- Phase 2: broaden + add policy templates in Console.
- Phase 3: consider default-on for new routes that meet traffic thresholds.

Immediate next steps (for me)
- Confirm defaults with Sean/Rafael + Allison (especially minimum traffic + warm-up + baseline semantics).
- Sync with Ethan/Benji on what’s realistic for v1 monitor query + caching.
- Get Chloe/Jada to react to UX “verdict + history + override” endpoints.
- Write the Confluence PRD draft using this as raw material.

Meeting notes / reminders (messy)
- From eng-platform thread: there’s concern that “warm-up delay” can hide real regressions; we need to pick a number that doesn’t look arbitrary.
- From eng-sre thread: cooldown must exist; also suggest “N of M” evaluation rather than single threshold crossing.
- From architecture thread: don’t tie rollback to a single provider/monitoring backend; we need standardized monitor identities.

Loose ends / parking lot
- How do we expose “policy templates” in Console without overwhelming users?
- Do we allow per-route policy overrides for self-serve customers (Hosted) or keep it enterprise-only initially?
- Should we add “rollback reason categories” for analytics (latency breach vs error breach vs unknown/monitor issue)?
- Are there any legal/compliance constraints on auto actions changing traffic without explicit human approval? (likely ok if auditable + documented, but check with Naomi).
